The cross-sectional momentum strategy for the Indian equity market aims to capitalize on the tendency for stocks with strong past performance (momentum) to continue outperforming in the near future. This phenomenon persists due to persistent investor sentiment and behavioral biases, as well as the惯性in underlying economic fundamentals.

To exploit this mechanism, the rule would identify a subset of stocks with the highest positive return momentum over a recent period (e.g., 6-12 months). These selected stocks would be weighted by their historical performance for long positions. Short positions could be taken on underperforming stocks to hedge market exposure or due to expected reversals in weak momentum. Rebalancing the portfolio periodically ensures adaptation to changing market conditions while maintaining the momentum advantage.

The signal for this cross-sectional momentum strategy can be derived by computing the cumulative returns over a specific lookback period (e.g., 6-12 months) from daily open, high, low, close prices. Volume data can be used to filter out noisy stocks or those with liquidity issues. On a given day, candidates are ranked based on their positive return momentum scores. The formula for the momentum score could be:

\[ \text{Momentum Score} = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T} (R_t - R^*)}{\sqrt{T}} \]

where \( R_t \) is the daily return of stock \( t \), \( R^* \) is the mean return over the lookback period, and \( T \) is the number of days in the lookback period. Stocks with higher momentum scores are selected for long positions, while those with lower or negative scores may be considered for short positions to hedge market exposure or capture expected reversals.

This strategy typically holds a concentrated portfolio of around 20-30 stocks to leverage momentum effectively. Positions can be weighted by their momentum scores, with higher weights given to top-ranked stocks. Risk limits can include holding no more than 5% in any single stock and limiting the total short positions to no more than 10% of the portfolio value to manage exposure. Loss bounds might cap individual losses at -20% per stock to prevent significant drawdowns, ensuring a balanced risk profile.
